newsitem.title: USA: Clinton extends Gulf War illness inquiry.
newsitem.headline: Clinton extends Gulf War illness inquiry.

text.p: President Bill Clinton asked a panel of experts on Tuesday to extend its work on Gulf War illness and ordered other steps to help veterans stricken with undiagnosed ailments after the 1991 conflict with Iraq.

He acted after getting a report from a panel of scientists and defence experts that severely criticised the Pentagon's initial handling of the problem even though it supported the Pentagon's ultimate conclusion that there is no single cause for Gulf War Syndrome.

"We haven't ended the suffering, we don't have all the answers, and I won't be satisfied until we have done everything humanly possible to find them," Clinton said. "We will do whatever it takes to determine the cause of Gulf War illness."
As many as 60,000 of the more than 500,000 U.S. troops who served in the Gulf have complained of illnesses ranging from memory loss to fatigue and muscle and joint pain.

"Based on existing scientific data, none of the individual environmental Gulf War risk factors commonly suspected appears to be the cause. .. and while the committee finds that stress is likely to be an important contributing factor to Gulf War veterans illnesses, the story is by no means complete," said Dr. Joyce Lashof, who chairs the Presidential Advisory Committee on Gulf War Veterans' Illnesses.
Besides asking the panel to stay in business for another nine months, Clinton directed the Department of Veterans Affairs to consider extending its two-year time limit on disability claims.
He also directed Veterans Affairs and the Departments of Defence and Health and Human Services to develop "concrete, specific action plans" to follow the recommendations of the advisory panel.

"I pledge to our veterans and to every American: we will not stop until we have done all we can to care for our Gulf War veterans, to find out why they are sick, and to help make them healthy again," Clinton said.

The Pentagon has said it found no common cause for the complaints and no firm evidence that troops suffered from any exposure to Iraqi chemical or biological agents in the war, which saw a U.S.-led coalition drive Iraqi troops from Kuwait.

It also said there is no evidence that Iraq even used chemical arms in the war, but conceded last year that as many as 20,000 U.S. troops might have been been exposed to nerve agents in the March 1991 destruction of an Iraqi arms dump.

That destruction of ammunition by U.S. military engineers at Kamisiyah in southern Iraq sent up a giant blast cloud, and the Pentagon was now investigating whether U.S. soldiers suffered low-level exposure from fallout.
Some members of Congress and veterans groups, noting that the Kamisiyah incident was not revealed until recently, have accused the department of bumbling and even outright coverup.
Lashof said she and her colleagues found no evidence of a coverup. But she was critical of the Pentagon nonetheless.

"Overall, the government has responded with a comprehensive series of measures to resolve questions about Gulf War illnesses. Unfortunately, the positive nature of these efforts has been diminished by how the Department of Defence approached the possibility that U.S. troops had been exposed to chemical weapons," she said.
The Pentagon last month launched a new $2.5 million effort which will include a close look at the effects of low-level exposure to chemical agents.
But defence analysts say they expect the controversy over complaints from Gulf War troops, which is also going on in Britain, to continue for years.

Clinton, who will serve as president until January 2001, agreed that definitive answers probably will not be known for years. "My successor will be working on this. We will be monitoring this for a long time to come," he said.
